head:
Act · Dose

How much exercise to live longer

Between the 150 minutes a week, the 10,000 steps, the marathon runners and those who say a little walking is enough, it is easy to feel lost. This article goes step by step, starting from what the very large studies of whole populations say, to arrive at what you can concretely do with your time.

The question

The question

How much physical activity is associated with a longer life: from what point it starts, where it stops, and what can you do with it at your own scale?

Why ask the question? Because the messages you receive contradict each other. One official rule says 150 minutes a week. Another, very popular, says 10,000 steps a day. Magazines promise results from 10 minutes of intense effort. And in the other direction, you hear that extreme exercise would wear out the heart and that it is better not to overdo it.

All of them are about dose, but nobody shows you where the numbers come from, so you cannot know whether they apply to you.

Yet there is a serious answer, built on hundreds of thousands of people followed for years. It is not perfect, and we will say precisely where it stops. But it can be rebuilt step by step, and understood rather than believed. That is what this article does: each step starts from a claim, shows the evidence, then examines what could distort it before moving on to the next, more precise one.

What is at stake

What is at stake first is lifespan, and that is what these studies measure, because death is the hardest outcome to dispute. According to a 2012 estimate published in The Lancet, physical inactivity would be responsible for about 9% of premature deaths worldwide, that is more than 5.3 million deaths out of 57 million in 2008 (range 5.1 to 12.5%).4 In the same analysis, it accounts for about 6% of coronary heart disease, 7% of type 2 diabetes, 10% of breast cancers and 10% of colon cancers.4 These are model-based estimates, not counts.

The same work calculates that eliminating inactivity would add 0.68 years of life expectancy to the world population (range 0.41 to 0.95). This figure is an average across everyone, including those who already move. Do not read it as what you would gain yourself.

Then there is what these studies do not measure, but which matters to you: staying independent, sleeping well, not feeling discouraged, performing if you compete. They only cover mortality and a few diseases. This has to be said from the outset, so as not to make them say more than they do.

Finally, there is a decision at stake. If you believe that less than 150 minutes is useless, you risk doing nothing at all, in the week when your schedule does not allow it. If you believe that more is always better, you may sacrifice sleep or recovery for a gain the studies do not show. And if you want to train hard, you have the right to know whether longevity justifies easing off. The question therefore cannot be left unanswered: it determines how you spread your time.
rest:
The demonstration

Six steps, from the most general to the most precise: the shape of the curve across a whole population, its lower end, the same thing with a measuring device, particular situations, what goes beyond endurance, then the objections.

Step 1 of 6

The relationship is not a straight line

Claim: the gain is greatest at the start, it continues, then it stops.

Researchers express activity as multiples of a recommended minimum: 2.5 hours of moderate effort per week (brisk walking, for example) or 1.25 hours of vigorous effort, which is the 150 minutes you have heard about.1 This minimum is a graduated rule. It does not say that nothing happens below it.

The evidence comes from an analysis of 6 large American and European cohorts: 661,137 adults with a median age of 62 years, followed for a median of 14.2 years, during which 116,686 died.2 Leisure-time activity (walking, running, cycling, swimming, dancing, tennis) was self-reported by questionnaire, and the results are adjusted for smoking, alcohol, BMI, medical history and other factors.13 Each level is compared with people who report no activity.

The risk of death falls from small volumes onwards, then the gain stops

Reduction = 1 minus the published risk ratio (0.80; 0.69; 0.63; 0.61; 0.69), so derived, rounded figures. The 5 to 10 times category is not in the sources read. Source: Arem et al., JAMA Internal Medicine, 2015, based on [1] and [2].

What this means

A volume below the minimum is already associated with a risk of death about 20% lower. Between one and two times the minimum, it reaches 31%. The peak, at 39%, is at 3 to 5 times the minimum. The first step is therefore the most rewarding: if you start from zero, you do not have to wait until you reach 150 minutes for it to count.

This peak is nothing like an athletic feat: according to the authors, it corresponds to about 7 hours of walking per week, or 5 hours of easy cycling, that is roughly one hour of walking a day (derived calculation).1 The American College of Cardiology report adds that the curve is slightly steeper for cardiovascular mortality than for cancer.3 And at 10 times the minimum or more, there is neither additional benefit nor increased risk: “no additional mortality benefit, but also no increased risk of death”.1

Transition. This curve comes from people who, for the most part, already move enough. That leaves the very bottom, where most of the people who lack time or motivation are found: what happens with truly tiny doses?

Step 2 of 6

The bottom of the scale matters more than you think

Claim: volumes far below the minimum are already associated with a lower risk, measured in three ways.

Minutes. In Taiwan, a cohort of 416,175 adults, followed for about 8 years, was divided into five activity levels. The lowest active level, about 15 minutes a day or 92 minutes a week, is associated with a 14% lower risk of all-cause death, a 10% lower risk of death from cancer and about 3 more years of life expectancy than the inactive. Each additional 15-minute block reduces the risk by a further 4% or so.5 Put another way: the inactive had a 17% higher risk than this group that moves for a quarter of an hour a day.5 The most important difference is between nothing and a little.

Steps. A meta-analysis of 15 cohorts followed 47,471 adults (3,013 deaths, median follow-up of 7.1 years) whose daily steps were measured.6 It splits them into four groups of equal size, from the least to the most active, whose median daily steps are 3,553, 5,801, 7,842 and 10,901.

The risk drops from the first few thousand steps, then the curve flattens

All-cause mortality risk ratio, with the least active group (median 3,553 steps) set at 1. Points placed at the median steps of each group; plateaus by age as published. Source: Paluch et al., Lancet Public Health, 2022, based on the report [6].

What this means

Going from about 3,500 to about 5,800 steps a day comes with a 40% lower risk of death (0.60, derived calculation), which is most of the total reduction, reaching 53% in the most active quarter. After 60, the plateau starts earlier: between 6,000 and 8,000 steps, against 8,000 to 10,000 before 60.6 What this means for you: the figure of 10,000 steps is a round benchmark, not a threshold. The same report points out that this figure comes from a Japanese commercial pedometer campaign, not from a study.6

Another study, American (4,840 adults aged 40 and over, followed for about ten years), finds the same shape: at 8,000 steps a day, the risk of death is 50% lower than in the 4,000-step group, and 65% lower at 12,000 steps.7

Efforts of a few seconds. What if you do not move at all, and do not want to start? A UK Biobank study covered 25,241 people who do no exercise, fitted with a wrist sensor, followed for 6.9 years on average (852 deaths). An intense effort of 1 to 2 minutes, for example climbing stairs quickly or picking up the pace, repeated about 3 times a day, is associated with a 38 to 40% lower risk of death; for a total of about 4.4 minutes a day, the reduction is 26 to 30% for all-cause and cancer mortality.8 Caution: few deaths, short duration, simple association. It is a clue, not a prescription.

Transition. Three different measures (minutes, steps, brief efforts) give the same shape. But two of them rely on what people say about themselves. Let us see whether the shape holds when a device does the counting.

Step 3 of 6

The shape of the curve holds when a device measures

Claim: the effect does not come from a reporting bias, since it is found with an accelerometer.

We remember poorly what we have done, and we tend to embellish. A meta-analysis of 8 studies therefore had 36,383 adults wear an accelerometer (mean age 62.6 years, 72.8% women) and tracked their deaths: 2,149 over a median of 5.8 years.9 Participants are divided into four equal groups; the least active serves as the reference.

The biggest drop in risk occurs between the first and second quarter

All-cause mortality risk ratio, main model; the first quarter is set at 1. Source: Ekelund et al., BMJ, 2019 [9].

What this means

Moving from the least active quarter to the next lowers the risk from 1.00 to 0.64: about three quarters of the total reduction observed at the top (36 points out of 48, derived calculation). The next two quarters add only a little. And light activity, the kind that is not sport, is also associated with a lower risk. What this means for you: walking, taking the stairs, standing counts, even if you do not consider yourself sporty.

The authors also give orders of magnitude in time. Between the least active quarter and the next, the gap is about 5 minutes a day of moderate to vigorous effort, and about 60 minutes a day of light activity. The maximum reduction in risk is observed at around 24 minutes a day of moderate to vigorous effort, that is about 170 minutes a week (derived calculation).9 With a measuring instrument, we find the same order of magnitude as the 150 minutes of the rule.

That leaves the question of intensity: do you need to go fast for it to count? The results on steps are nuanced. In the American study, once the total number of steps is taken into account, pace adds nothing.7 In the meta-analysis of 15 cohorts, time spent walking at a brisk pace brings no significant further reduction, but the best 30 minutes of the day are associated with a risk ratio of 0.67, with total steps taken into account.6 Keep in mind that volume matters first, and that intensity is still a debated subject.

Transition. These averages hold for whole groups. But you are not the average: you may have a desk job, a schedule that allows only one or two sessions, or an age that does not match that of the cohorts. Let us look at these situations.

Step 4 of 6

Depending on your situation: sitting days, schedule, age

Claim: the dose adapts to how you live, but the broad lines remain.

If you spend your day sitting. Sitting time is associated with risk separately from sport. In the accelerometer study, the risk of death rises with sitting time: 1.28, 1.71, then 2.63 for the three most sedentary quarters, compared with the least sedentary. It increases gradually from 7.5 to 9 hours a day, faster beyond 9.5 hours, and reaches 2.92 at 12 hours a day.9 These values do not add up with those for activity: each line comes from a separate model.

Can you compensate? An analysis of 16 studies, over a million people, cross-tabulated sitting time and activity. It concludes that 60 to 75 minutes of moderate activity a day is enough to cancel the excess risk linked to sitting 8 hours or more. Inactive people had a risk of death 28 to 59% higher than the most active quarter, whatever their sitting time.10 This figure exceeds the minimum, so it does not apply to everyone: it answers a specific case, that of a sedentary job. For you, that means the evening walk or the morning ride is not a bonus, it serves as a counterweight.

If you only have two slots a week. A British study (63,591 adults, mean age almost 59 years, 8,802 deaths) compared people who concentrate their activity into one or two sessions a week, while reaching 150 minutes of moderate or 75 minutes of vigorous activity, with the inactive. Their risk of all-cause death is about 30% lower, that of cardiovascular death 40% lower and that of death from cancer 18% lower.11 The total therefore seems to matter more than the distribution. Activity was self-reported and over 90% of participants were white, so generalisation is limited.11

Depending on your age. The cohorts cited are mostly made up of adults with a median or mean age of 59 to 63 years where stated. Steps are the only result read that distinguishes age groups, with a plateau that arrives earlier after 60. For a 25-year-old adult, these studies do not allow the figures to be extended mechanically.

Transition. So far, we have talked about endurance: walking, running, cycling. But that is not the only way to exert yourself, nor the only thing the studies have measured.

Step 5 of 6

Endurance is not everything: strength training and fitness

Claim: strength training adds to endurance, and measured fitness is also very strongly associated with lifespan.

A meta-analysis of 16 cohort studies looked at strength training alone. People who do it have a 15% lower risk of all-cause death than those who do not (0.85; 7 studies, 263,058 participants), and a lower risk of cardiovascular disease (0.83), of cancer overall (0.88) and of diabetes (0.83). Those who combine strength training and endurance have a 40% lower risk of death than those who do neither (0.60; 3 studies, 581,194 participants).12

Strength training alone is associated with a lower risk, the combination with endurance with a much lower one

Reduction = 1 minus the published relative risk (0.85; 0.83; 0.88; 0.83; 0.60), so derived. The first four bars compare strength training with none; the last compares strength training plus endurance with neither, from other studies. Source: Momma et al., British Journal of Sports Medicine, 2022 [12].

What this means

Strength training is associated with fewer deaths, but also with fewer cancers and less diabetes: it does not replace walking, it adds to it. For the dose, the meta-analysis finds the lowest risks at around 30 to 60 minutes per week, with curves that flatten or rise again afterwards. The authors judge the certainty of this evidence to be very low for mortality: take these minutes as a benchmark, not as a proven dose.12

One question remains: at bottom, it may be fitness rather than volume that counts. An American study measured, on a treadmill, the exercise capacity of 122,007 patients, followed for a median of 8.4 years (13,637 deaths). The top performers (the best 2.3% of their age class) have a risk of death about 80% lower than the lowest performers. The authors compare the risk of low fitness with that of smoking, diabetes and coronary heart disease, and judge it comparable or greater.13 After 70, the very high performers still have a 29% lower risk than the “high performers” (0.71; interval 0.52 to 0.98).13

This study has to be read with care: these are patients from a single hospital, sent for a stress test, so not the general population, and fitness comes both from what you do and from what you are (age, genetics, health). But it gives the rationale for a fitness test: volume is what you control, fitness is what you can check, and the two are not the same thing.

Transition. Everything so far is consistent. That is precisely the moment to be wary: a demonstration that meets no objection is not one.

Step 6 of 6

What can distort the demonstration, and what remains uncertain

Objection 1: sick people move less. This is reverse causation: it would not be inactivity that makes people ill, but illness that makes them inactive. The authors of the accelerometer study excluded deaths from the first two years; the results do not change notably, apart from a small attenuation for sitting time. They themselves state that this bias may remain.9

Objection 2: active people are different. They smoke less, eat differently, have better access to healthcare. The studies adjust for these factors, without ever erasing them completely: the authors speak of possible residual confounding.9

Objection 3: measurement is not always good. The studies by Arem, from Taiwan and by Momma rely on questionnaires, and the Arem sample has only 8% completely inactive people and seems more active than the general population.3 The device-based studies measure activity only once, in the United States and Western Europe.9

Objection 4: people were not assigned at random. The most cited randomised trial on the subject, Generation 100 in Norway (about 1,500 older adults), compared high-intensity interval training, moderate training and a control group. At 5 years, all-cause mortality is 3%, 6% and 4.5%. The difference between intervals and moderate is not statistically significant, and about one participant in five in the control group trained on their own at high intensity.14 This trial therefore does not show that training makes you live longer than inactivity, because its comparison group was not inactive. Among the sources read for this article, no randomised trial establishes the effect of dose on mortality. The argument rests on the consistency between many observational studies, not on an experiment.

Objection 5: is the ceiling a real ceiling? The graph in step 1 suggests that beyond 3 to 5 times the minimum, more is of no use. Let us look at the margins of error.

At the top, we cannot decide between “the same” and “a little worse”

All-cause mortality risk ratio (inactive = 1) and 95% confidence interval. Scale truncated from 0.55 to 0.85 to show the width of the intervals. The coloured band is the interval of the group at 3 to 5 times the minimum. Source: Arem et al., based on the Heart report [2].

What this means

For each group up to the peak, the interval is narrow: these differences are real in the data. The group at 10 times the minimum or more, however, has a very wide interval (0.59 to 0.78) because it is small (4,077 people, 212 deaths according to the ACC commentary, which does not say whether this category matches exactly).3 Its interval overlaps the peak and also the “1 to 2 times” zone: the study cannot say whether doing a very great deal is better, the same or slightly worse. The absence of danger is a cautious result, not proof of safety for you. And these studies cover neither injuries, nor heart rhythm disorders, nor overtraining.

The answer to the question

The question was: how much activity is associated with a longer life, from what point, up to where, and what can you do with it? Here is the answer, with the level of certainty of each piece.

What is solid. The direction of the relationship: more active people die less, in all the studies read, however activity is measured (questionnaire, pedometer, accelerometer) and whatever the population. The shape too: the slope is steepest between nothing and a little, and there is no threshold below which nothing happens.

What is probable. Most of the gain comes with a dose close to the minimum: about 150 to 300 moderate minutes per week (31% lower risk in the Arem study), and the reduction continues up to 3 to 5 times this minimum (about an hour of walking a day) before levelling off. In steps, this corresponds to 6,000 to 8,000 a day after 60, 8,000 to 10,000 before. To this are added benchmarks for strength training, and the fact that this dose can be spread out, including into one or two sessions.

What remains uncertain. Whether it is the activity itself that causes the gain: all the data are observational, and no randomised trial has been read that settles it. The exact dose of strength training. The role of intensity. What happens beyond 10 times the minimum. And above all, what these group averages mean for a specific person. If someone promises you a number of years gained, the promise goes beyond the data.

Short answer: there is no minimum dose below which it is of no use. The first tens of minutes are the most rewarding, 150 minutes a week is a good target, and beyond about an hour a day of moderate effort the studies no longer show any longevity gain, nor any danger.

What you can put in place

Here is an ordered way to turn these results into a week. It is a construction based on the studies, not a tested protocol. If you have an illness, an injury or a doubt, ask a doctor for advice before increasing the dose.

  1. Start small, without waiting until you have time.A quarter of an hour of brisk walking a day (92 minutes a week) is the level associated with a 14% lower risk in Taiwan.5 If you do nothing today, this is your first step, and it is the most rewarding.
  2. Work up towards 150 minutes a week of moderate effort.For example 5 times 30 minutes. If your schedule leaves you only one or two slots, concentrate them: the total seems to matter more than the distribution.11 Every minute below this threshold is still associated with a benefit.
  3. Track your steps too.Aim for 6,000 to 8,000 steps a day if you are over 60, 8,000 to 10,000 if you are younger.6 These are the observed plateaus, not targets to exceed at all costs.
  4. Add strength training two days a week.This is the WHO recommendation, which asks for activities working the major muscle groups on at least two days a week.15 The 30 to 60 minutes a week from the meta-analysis are a benchmark, with weak evidence.12
  5. If your day is spent sitting, compensate.Break up sitting time, and aim for the order of 60 to 75 minutes of walking or cycling a day when possible: this is what cancels the excess risk associated with sitting 8 hours or more in the analysis of 16 studies.10
  6. Measure your fitness, not just your volume.Take the Fitness test on this page now: it places your current level, without measuring your volume (it is not the treadmill test from the study cited above). Retake it every two to three months, a pace that is a coaching benchmark and not a study result, to see whether your level moves, and keep track yourself of your weekly minutes and steps.

If you already train a lot, nothing in these studies invites you to cut back in order to live longer, and nothing shows that more would bring you extra years. What you are looking for elsewhere, performance, enjoyment, competition, is not in these data.

What these figures do not say
  • Association, not cause. All these studies observe people, except one trial whose control group was not inactive.
  • Only mortality and a few diseases are measured: not performance, nor injuries, nor quality of life.
  • These figures describe group averages, not what will happen to you.

Frequently asked questions

I don't have 150 minutes. Is it still worth it?

The data say yes several times over: about 20% lower risk below the minimum in Arem, 14% at 92 minutes a week in Taiwan, 40% at 5,800 steps a day.256 These are associations between groups, not a promise of a gain for you.

Do sessions need to last at least 10 minutes?

No. The 2020 WHO recommendations dropped this rule: activity in bouts of any length counts.15

If I already train a lot, should I cut back?

These studies do not suggest it: they show no increased risk, only the absence of additional longevity gain beyond 3 to 5 times the minimum, with limited precision.13
